paras: The lynching of Tom Johnson was the killing of a Black man by a mob near Hattiesburg, Mississippi, on Friday, July 26, 1895. Accused of an ax and pistol attack on the Hartfield family, he was taken from jail, escaped, was recaptured and was shot to death before a large crowd after a reported confession. Mississippi papers praised the killing, digests elsewhere turned it into a burning, and the New-York Tribune ridiculed it.

According to the Pascagoula Democrat-Star, on the night of July 20 Katie and Susie Hartfield, aged 14 and 16, were struck with an ax at their home near Hattiesburg, Susie was "outraged," and their mother was shot three times. One of the girls died; a Jackson dispatch placed the house sixteen miles southwest of town and called Johnson "an ex-convict." Armed parties hunted him until an elderly man named Reddoch, his son and his nephew took him at a cabin, though other reports placed the capture at Ellisville or in Covington county. He was lodged in the jail at Hattiesburg.

A Meridian dispatch said a crowd demanded the prisoner and, when the sheriff refused, knocked a hole through the jail wall, broke about seven locks, and shot Johnson several times when he "showed fight" with a crowbar. The New Orleans Daily States put the mob at 100 men, the Jackson dispatch at 200, and both dated the seizure to Wednesday. On the way to the Hartfield place he escaped and was recaptured Thursday afternoon, after a twelve hours' search with bloodhounds by the Jackson account.

On Friday morning his captors reached the Hartfield home, where, according to the Jackson dispatch, Mrs. Hartfield said, "That's the man who shot me." The same dispatch said he offered to confess if promised he would not be burned or tortured, naming robbery as his motive and saying he acted alone. A "committee" was appointed and Johnson was allowed to choose his manner of death; he chose shooting. At about 2 o'clock he was shot "in the presence of an immense crowd," tied between two saplings, with over one thousand shots by the Pascagoula count and "upward of five hundred" by the Tribune's.

No participant was named; the Pascagoula Democrat-Star called them "the best and most prominent citizens of Perry county." The Free Press noted that "there was no effort at concealment," and no report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution appears in the coverage.

Mississippi papers openly approved. The Pascagoula Democrat-Star headed its account "Horrible! A Negro Fiend Knocks Two Young Ladies in the Head With a Hatchet" and said in an editorial that Johnson "got what he richly deserved" and "His kind will always meet a similar fate." The Southern Herald, quoting the Gazette, called him "The negro brute" whose body was "pierced by hundreds of bullets" fired "by the citizens of the community."

Outside the state, the Daily States special ran under "Was Not Burned, But Literally Riddled with Bullets for His Crime" in the Monticellonian, the Cape Girardeau Democrat and the News Boy, and in the Fisherman & Farmer of Edenton, North Carolina. Digest columns such as the Hope Pioneer's instead placed the crime at Meridian and said Johnson was "burned at the stake," and one Kentucky brief put Hattiesburg in Tennessee.

On August 11 the New-York Tribune wrote that the lynching party "politely gave him the privilege" of choosing his death and that the local paper "extols the neat manner in which the job was done." Outside Mississippi, it concluded, there was "little admiration for the incident."

The only report found in a paper addressed to Black readers ran on August 10 in the Weekly Call of Kansas, in an "About Our People" column beside news of Black schools and the London anti-lynching committee. It condensed the Daily States account without comment.

Most reports dated the shooting Friday, July 26, but the Free Press wrote "last Saturday evening" and counted "500 or more" men. Early reports said Mrs. Hartfield and a daughter, or two girls, had been killed, while the fuller Mississippi accounts reported one daughter dead and the mother wounded. The digest story of a burning is contradicted by every detailed report.

reader.title: Lynching of Tom Johnson
bases: A mob took Johnson from the Hattiesburg jail, recaptured him after an escape, and shot him to death before a crowd after he was identified and said to have confessed (A6, A12, A14).

Johnson was shot to death by a mob of 100 to 500 men who broke him out of jail against the sheriff's refusal (A1, A3, A12, A14); they acted on an accusation of murder and assault, staging identification, a 'committee' and a confession before the killing (A6, A14).

Independent Hattiesburg dispatches via New Orleans (A12), Jackson (A14) and Meridian (A1), plus the Mississippi weeklies (A3, A6, A9), agree that a mob took Johnson from jail and killed him; only digest briefs (A10) say he was burned rather than shot.

accounts.label: New Orleans Daily States special
accounts.gist: Mob of 100 took Johnson from jail Wednesday night; he escaped, was recaptured Thursday, identified and confessed, and was riddled with bullets in the woods before an immense crowd Friday afternoon.

accounts.label: Jackson dispatch
accounts.gist: Ex-convict Johnson, captured in Covington county, was taken from jail by 200 men, recaptured with bloodhounds, identified by Mrs. Hartfield, and confessed on a promise not to be burned or tortured.

accounts.label: Meridian dispatch (before the killing)
accounts.gist: Citizens broke through the jail wall after the sheriff refused them; Johnson fought with a crowbar and was shot several times; burning was talked of.

accounts.label: Pascagoula Democrat-Star (local Mississippi account)
accounts.gist: Detailed the July 20 attack, the capture by Reddoch, the jail break, escape and recapture, a committee, and over a thousand shots fired into Johnson tied between saplings.

accounts.label: Confession as printed (obtained in mob custody)
accounts.gist: A signed statement attributed to Johnson admits the Hartfield attack and two robberies, says no one was with him, and denies two other killings.

accounts.label: Digest columns
accounts.gist: Briefs placed the crime at Meridian and said the mob burned Johnson at the stake.

framing.detail: Pascagoula Democrat-Star: 'Horrible! A Negro Fiend...' and an editorial saying Johnson 'got what he richly deserved'; the Southern Herald's Gazette paragraph called him 'The negro brute'.
Big Sandy News and St. Tammany Farmer: 'paid the penalty ... at the hands of a well directed mob'; 'the negro murderer and rapist'.
Daily States special, headed 'Was Not Burned, But Literally Riddled with Bullets for His Crime', reprinted without comment.
Weekly digest briefs garbled the place and manner (Meridian; burned at the stake; Tennessee).
New-York Tribune editorial mocked the 'fine politeness' of the ceremony and the 'grade of civilization' of Mississippi.
Weekly Call's 'About Our People' column condensed the Daily States account without comment.

conflicts.note: The detailed Hattiesburg, Jackson and Mississippi accounts all say shooting; the burning version appears only in distant digest briefs, which also misplace the crime at Meridian.
Dated dispatches of July 27 already report the killing as 'yesterday', supporting Friday.
Figures may refer to different moments (jail break vs. the killing).
